solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Son remains in more than one band (6)

blocks.note: S = son, as in family-tree notation

explanation.surface: A grieving family has a son's remains buried among the members of several bands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Band' reads as a group of musicians, but here it is a strip of cloth worn across the body.
explanation.definitionFit: A sash is a band of cloth, so several of them are more than one band.

clue.text: Oil producer unchanged after surprise on vacation (6)

indicators.note: after means coming later in the line, so SAME is written behind SE
a word on vacation is emptied of its middle, leaving its outer letters

blocks.note: SurprisE with its inside emptied leaves S…E

explanation.surface: An oil producer's output stays flat after a surprise announcement made while on holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oil producer' suggests a company or a country; it is the plant whose seeds are pressed for sesame oil.
explanation.definitionFit: Sesame seeds are pressed to make sesame oil, so the plant produces oil.

clue.text: I let my helpers cast child star (7,6)

indicators.note: to cast is to throw, so the letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A director lets assistants choose the cast for a film with a child star.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast' sits naturally beside 'star' as film talk, which hides that it is the anagram instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Shirley Temple was the most famous child film star of 1930s Hollywood.

clue.text: Cross taken from outside is everlasting (7)

indicators.note: X is removed from the word that follows

blocks.note: X = a cross, the letter that is taken out

explanation.surface: A cross removed from outside a church turns out to be a permanent fixture.
explanation.walkthrough: X is the crossword's standard cross, as in a mark on a ballot paper.
explanation.definitionFit: Eternal and everlasting both mean lasting for ever.

clue.text: Ignore idiot bitten by young dog (4,2)

indicators.note: the dog's jaws close around the idiot, so PUP goes around ASS

blocks.note: a pup is a young dog

explanation.surface: Someone is told to ignore a fool who has just been bitten by a puppy.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as advice, so 'Ignore' looks like an instruction rather than the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A phrasal-verb synonym: you pass up an offer by declining to take any notice of it.

clue.text: Bend over following a cold in African city (5)

indicators.note: in a down clue, over flips the word upward
to follow is to come behind, so CRA is written after A and C

blocks.note: C = cold, as on a tap

explanation.surface: Someone doubles over with a cold caught in an African city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bend over' looks like a single phrasal verb, but 'over' is the instruction to turn ARC round.
explanation.definitionFit: Accra is the capital of Ghana, in West Africa.

clue.text: Old rhino eating pine cone’s top is horrifying (5-8)

indicators.note: SHILLING takes PINE C inside it
in a down clue the top of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: rhino is old British slang for money; a shilling is a pre-1971 British coin

explanation.surface: An ancient rhinoceros chomps on a pine cone, and the sight is horrifying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rhino' is dated British slang for money, so 'old rhino' is a coin of the old money, the shilling, worth twelve pence.
explanation.definitionFit: Something spine-chilling sends a shiver of fear down the back, so it is horrifying.

clue.text: Father and young adult in tree (6)

blocks.note: YA = young adult, the publishing category

explanation.surface: A father and his teenage child are up a tree together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' reads as up in the branches; it only links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The papaya is a tropical tree grown for its fruit.

clue.text: Broadcast entertaining recommendation for allowance (7)

indicators.note: to entertain a guest is to hold them, so SEND holds TIP

blocks.note: to send a signal is to broadcast it

explanation.surface: A broadcaster airs an entertaining programme recommending what to do with an allowance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' looks like an anagram instruction; here it is a verb meaning send.
explanation.definitionFit: A stipend is a fixed regular payment, an allowance.

clue.text: Eats a meal around some weird state capital (3,6)

indicators.note: DINES goes around the rearranged letters
a weird version of SOME is a jumbled one

blocks.note: to dine is to eat a meal

explanation.surface: Someone eats a meal surrounded by strange sights in a state capital.
explanation.walkthrough: Des Moines is the capital of Iowa, a US state.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Iowa's seat of government sits in Des Moines, one of fifty US state capitals.

clue.text: Fast food item enthralling male primate (5)

indicators.note: to enthral is to hold captive, so CHIP holds M

blocks.note: a chip is a piece of fried potato

explanation.surface: A chip from a takeaway fascinates a male ape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Enthralling' looks like praise for the food; it is the instruction to put M inside CHIP.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the chimpanzee, shortened here, is one of the great apes in the primate order.

clue.text: Lemon is fresh fruit (5)

indicators.note: a fresh version of a word is a new arrangement of it

explanation.surface: A greengrocer's claim that the lemon is fresh fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is so plain that 'Lemon' looks like the definition; the answer is a different fruit made from its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the melon is a large sweet fruit of the gourd family, and the clue swaps one fruit for another.

clue.text: State stopping clandestine servitude (7)

indicators.note: AVER is put in like a stopper, plugging SLY

blocks.note: to aver is to state firmly

explanation.surface: A government moves to stop secret forced labour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State' reads as a nation; here it is the verb meaning declare.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both name the state of being owned by or bound to serve another person.

clue.text: Slightly cowardly cry over desire (9)

blocks.note: O = over, the cricket scoring abbreviation

explanation.surface: A timid person whimpers over something they want.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket an over is six balls bowled from one end, and scorecards abbreviate it to O.
explanation.definitionFit: Yellow means cowardly, and -ish makes it only slightly so.

clue.text: Blow up trendy apartment close to Knightsbridge (7)

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, its last letter

explanation.surface: A fashionable apartment near Knightsbridge is blown up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close to' reads as nearby, and it means the final letter. Knightsbridge is a wealthy London district.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: filling a tyre or balloon with air enlarges it, and 'blow up' here means that, not explode.

clue.text: Stole coat on the counter, partly for fur (6)

indicators.note: counter means running against, so the letters are read backwards
only part of the words is used

explanation.surface: A thief steals a coat from a shop counter, taking it for its fur.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stole' looks like a fur wrap and 'counter' like a shop's, which disguises both the fodder and the reversal.
explanation.definitionFit: The ocelot is a wild cat once widely hunted for its fur.

clue.text: One might be constricted by this skimpy thong, somewhat (6)

definitions.text: One might be constricted by this

indicators.note: only some of the words is used

explanation.surface: A skimpy thong is so tight it constricts its wearer.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes the thong the constrictor; the definition is really about a snake that crushes its prey.
explanation.definitionFit: A python kills by constriction, so its prey is constricted by it.

clue.text: Reduce value of collection housed in exhibition centre the wrong way (7)

indicators.note: HEAP lives inside the reversed centre
going the wrong way means travelling backwards, so NEC is read right to left

blocks.note: the NEC is the National Exhibition Centre in Birmingham
a heap is a collection of things

explanation.surface: A collection displayed at an exhibition centre loses value by being shown the wrong way round.
explanation.walkthrough: The NEC is the National Exhibition Centre, a large venue near Birmingham, England.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: making something cheap lowers what it is worth, in money or in esteem.

clue.text: Place of rest in a church (5)

blocks.note: per = a, as in fifty pence a head

explanation.surface: A resting place found inside a church, such as a pew or a grave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like the link word, but 'a' is the working part: PER as in 'miles per hour'.
explanation.definitionFit: A perch is where a bird rests.

clue.text: Silly act following foul play regularly ignored (5)

indicators.note: every other letter is dropped, starting with the first

blocks.note: f. = following, as in page references
fOuL pLaY, keeping the even letters

explanation.surface: A foolish act comes after foul play that the referee kept missing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Following' looks like an order word, but here it is the abbreviation F.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: folly means foolishness, and a single foolish deed can be called a folly.

clue.text: Outcast quietly wearing lascivious grin (5)

indicators.note: P wears LEER around it like a garment

blocks.note: a leer is a lewd grin

explanation.surface: A social outcast silently wears a lecherous grin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leper' is used figuratively for someone shunned by everyone.
explanation.definitionFit: A leper, figuratively, is a person everyone avoids, an outcast.

clue.text: Criticise one’s boring second husband from Madrid? (7)

indicators.note: PAN IS bores into S H, sitting inside them

blocks.note: to pan a film is to criticise it

explanation.surface: Someone complains that their second husband, from Madrid, is dull.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boring' reads as dull, the natural complaint about a husband; it means drilling into. The question mark flags that Madrid is just one example of Spain.
explanation.definitionFit: Something from Madrid is from Spain's capital, so it is Spanish.

clue.text: Produce canines, perhaps and support them, mostly (6)

indicators.note: most of the word is kept, losing its last letter

blocks.note: a golf tee supports the ball

explanation.surface: A kennel owner breeds dogs and pays for their keep, or most of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Canines' look like dogs; here they are pointed teeth. 'Perhaps' signals that canines are just one kind.
explanation.definitionFit: To teethe is to cut new teeth, canines among them.

clue.text: Rage corrupted a new American president (6)

indicators.note: a corrupted word has its letters spoiled into a new order

explanation.surface: Fury at a newly elected, corrupt American president.
explanation.walkthrough: Ronald Reagan was US president from 1981 to 1989.
explanation.definitionFit: Ronald Reagan was the 40th president of the United States.
